US secretary of state’s comments come as vulnerability in programming language Java highlighted
There is “zero evidence” that a wave of IT outages – which have grounded flights, cut off work access, limited bank access, affected Apple and disrupted classified communications – are related to each other or are the work of malign actors, according to the US secretary of state.
Marco Rubio said the US was “not under systemic attack” and a cascade of network problems was “not inter-related”.
In recent days, Microsoft , major US banks , Apple , American air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages.
“We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber-hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” Rubio said.
Rubio’s comments came as cybersecurity researchers flagged a vulnerability in Java, a programming language used by 90% of companies in the Fortune 500, a ranking of the largest companies in the US. The researchers at US-based Calif used AI to discover the flaw and recently unearthed glitches in PHP, another computer language.
Calif said the Java flaw could allow hackers to remotely execute code, allowing them to place malicious software on a target’s systems.
The US director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, said the incidents were caused by security upgrades – such as plugging the flaws in PHP – that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
“Everybody recognises it’s time to upgrade their systems, and as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases, and in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected,” he told the Fox Business news channel.
Tal Be’ery, a cybersecurity expert, said he did not believe the incidents were linked directly but had a common underlying theme: AI. IT systems were buckling under the pressure of adding AI or tackling flaws uncovered by AI, he said.
“Our IT infrastructure is brittle, and when AI puts massive extra pressure on it, whether through upgrades to accommodate AI or through the rapid patching that AI-driven vulnerability discovery demands,” Be’ery said.
Since April, when the AI startup Anthropic released its Mythos model, which had a startling ability to flag IT flaws, the amount of vulnerabilities found by leading tech companies has soared eightfold – while OpenAI has also released models capable of finding previously unseen flaws. Researchers at Calif used OpenAI technology to discover the Java flaw.
“[Java] is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Calif wrote in a blogpost . “Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.”
However, Steven Murdoch, a professor of security engineering at University College London, said the flaw did not apply to every Java user and was specific to a library of code – Base64 – that comes bundled with a version of Java.
“It’s significant but it’s not every Java program that is affected,” he said.
In the UK the National Cyber Security Centre urged organisations to keep their systems up to date, while the US and South Korean authorities also urged Java users to install security updates.
Rubio made the comments as he travelled with Donald Trump for key meetings in the Philippines on Wednesday, before flying to the tech hub of Shenzhen in China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the outages on Tuesday. “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” Trump said in Manila.
The series of outages began on Thursday last week, when Microsoft’s email and other tools went down , affecting millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the problem to “an earlier network capacity upgrade”.
Flights across the US were grounded the next day in the longest “ground stop” since the September 11 attacks. The US Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related”.
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
Then on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance”. Apple also confirmed problems with its iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday but said it had resolved them.
The Democrat Mark Warner, the vice-chair of the Senate intelligence committee, supported the assessment that the outages were not caused by a “coordinated effort” but by attempts to shore up systems.
“The evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity.”
Cynthia Kaiser, a former deputy director in the FBI’s cyber division, said it was “plausible” that the race to upgrade systems was fuelled by warnings that specific cyber adversaries were planning attacks.
Kaiser, now an executive at cybersecurity firm Halcyon, said she was more concerned about cyber criminals and scammers trying to “capitalise on the confusion to steal money from organisations and everyday people ”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took time during a high-level diplomatic summit in Asia on Wednesday to try and soothe public US jitters over a spate of cyber-related disruptions.
Rubio insisted authorities have found "zero evidence" that recent outages across tech platforms are related to one another or due to the work of "nefarious actors."
His comments, on the sidelines of a Southeast Asia summit, follow multiple disruptions of everything from US air traffic operations to Microsoft email and messaging to banking and mobile pay, as well as the outage of a top-secret US government communications network.
"The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever, we have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other," Rubio told reporters in Manila while on a trip to Asia with US President Donald Trump.
"The second is that we have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind."
Rubio emphasised the ubiquity of technology when explaining why it could feel as if there was a growing wave of cyber incidents.
"The more technology becomes embedded into our everyday lives, the more the vulnerabilities become real," he said.
"There was a time when people used to physically go in with masks and guns and rob banks. Now they can do it from behind a computer screen halfway around the world and every major economy in the world is facing that same challenge."
On Tuesday a top-secret network that the National Security Agency (NSA) uses for internal communications went down, the agency acknowledged.
The NSA said it had experienced "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," but that its capabilities remained operational and "our ability to defend national security continues."
The NSA, part of the US Department of Defence, is responsible for global monitoring, collection and processing of information for intelligence and counterintelligence.
The Trump administration has insisted Americans and their various systems remain secure, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin emphasizing that the wave of recent outages does not stem from cyber criminals.
"I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack," Mullin told CNBC. "There's no cyber threat that's taking place. The homeland is very secure."
Air travel was disrupted because of what the Trump administration called outdated equipment, causing regulators to halt all flights from taking off for several hours on Friday evening.
The mess of stranded travellers and aircrews spilled into the weekend and early this week.
Microsoft also suffered a major outage last week that affected Outlook and Teams users around the world, while several large banks saw disruptions to their banking apps and online portals on Monday.
Trump's rival Democratic Party, which just won decisively in US midterm elections earlier this month, blamed the administration's incompetence for the string of high-visibility outages and the lack of transparency around them.
"We've had the Microsoft incident, then we had the nationwide ground stop. Now we have concerns as it relates to highly classified servers over at the NSA," Hakeem Jeffries, a top Democrat in Congress, told reporters.
"I think it's time for the administration to come up to the Hill and explain themselves, so we can be informed about the steps that need to be taken and we can inform the people of the United States of America."

Meaning and use of word has become more important in age of AI chatbot, says dictionary
In a world where the line between people and machines is more blurred than ever, Cambridge dictionary has sided with natural intelligence for its word of the year: human.
Breakthroughs in artificial intelligence – led by the arrival of ChatGPT three years ago – have made the question of what it means to be human as vexed as ever, but the dictionary has drawn a firm line with its choice of the word of 2026, defining “human” as “having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines”.
AI advances have spurred questions about whether computers can achieve consciousness, with the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins among those who answered in the affirmative, saying he was “left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human”. Sceptics, on the other hand , argue that there is a vast difference between how a human brain evolves and how an AI system is built.
Cambridge dictionary said the meaning and use of “human” had become more important in the age of the chatbot. Colin McIntosh, an editor of the dictionary, said AI was “changing the way we talk about being human” and had led to the word of the year being deployed to distinguish our work from that of advanced computer systems. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking has made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children,” he said. “A recent increase in compounds such as ‘human-made’ highlight how the word has come to distinguish works or qualities of people, as distinct from AI.”
Prof Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said : “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.”
Other tech-related words were on the shortlist: “agent”, the term for an AI system that can operate – sometimes alarmingly – without human control, and “analogues”, relating to non-digital activities. A non-tech contender was “wholesome”, a word to describe something which is likely to improve your life either physically, morally, or emotionally.
Earlier this month, “mogging” – meaning to outperform or outshine someone or something – was named the Collins word of the year .
Tech-adjacent words also stood out among the new additions to the Cambridge dictionary. “Looksmaxxing”, describing the act of making oneself as physically attractive as possible, which has been associated with the online manosphere , and “aura farming”, another term often encountered on social media, which refers to “the activity of doing things with the intention of showing a personality that people admire and think is attractive and interesting”.
The former UK prime minister Keir Starmer made the news late last year when some social media users wondered “why he was aura farming” with his TikToks ; Andy Burnham also appears to be attempting to master the art after becoming prime minister.

"The growth of AI means it is now necessary to explicitly say 'human' for things that once could only be done by humans," said chief editor Colin McIntosh.
Examples of current usage included actors Scarlett Johansson challenging "an assault on human creativity" and Matthew McConaughey protecting himself against unauthorised digital reproduction of his voice or image.
"The measure of AI's success should be how much it improves human lives," said Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates on learning about the dictionary's choice.
McIntosh said dictionary editors had to be on top of how words could change over time "to reflect what people say and what they write".
His research revealed a four-fold use of the word human since 1900.
"'Man' used to be used in this sense a lot more, but now it is not acceptable to use 'man' to mean men and women," he added.
"Human didn't come into use in Middle English until the 14th Century, from a French word. Shakespeare used it, but after that it was very restricted in use."

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.
Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.
The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.
IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.
Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.
Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them
Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy ( documentation ). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.( documentation ). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.
The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.
See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:
Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.
A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.
Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.
Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.
Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.
- Scale model development . A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.
- Refresh predictions as data changes . Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.
- Put signals closer to decisions . Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.
- Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.
Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent
The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.
An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.
To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.
When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.
The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.
Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.
A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.
AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.
When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.
Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.
A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.
With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

I knew GTA was something special even before my mom punched me in the face.
This was an accident. She’s not much of a gamer, so the controls on the PS5 version of Grand Theft Auto Online are a bit of a mystery to her. She pressed the circle button, and her in-game character swung a giant punch that caught my character right in the head. Blood splattered. My mom cried out. My brother and I howled with laughter. She’d only been playing for a couple of hours, and she was already punching her kids. What a violent nightmare these games were.
GTA has been a part of my life since I was way too young to be playing it. My brother and I, aged 9 and 11-ish, discovered Grand Theft Auto 3 at a cool cousin’s house. We’d sit there, enraptured, cackling like gremlins and passing the controller back and forth every time one of us got WASTED. I remember wondering if video games could ever get more realistic.
Flash forward a couple of decades, and Grand Theft Auto VI releases on Thursday, a game poised to be the most lifelike, expansive title in the series— maybe in all of gaming . (The game apparently has a system for tracking your empathy.) It also has a real chance of becoming perhaps the highest-grossing entertainment property of all time.
People are very excited about this thing, so much so that there’s been hand-wringing about workplace productivity dropping because some 12.5 million people are taking time off to play the game. (It’s me; I am part of the problem. Please don’t tell my boss.)
Does that feel like too much hype for a video game? Not to me. Not when Grand Theft Auto has always been such a presence at very pivotal points in my life. It’s been much more than a flashy violence simulator.
My brother and I were the target demographic for these games. Vaguely inspired by gangster shoot-em-ups like Scarface , the GTA games have long been vehicles for male power fantasies. We got into them because you could run around and blow stuff up. Be chaotic. It was a good place to do that in, rather than, you know, the real world.
We also weren’t always that friendly when we entered adulthood. Lots of siblings aren’t all that close, especially as adults. When you live far away for long enough, phone calls and occasional visits can only do so much. The distance can be hard to close.
That really changed for us during the Covid-19 pandemic . My brother and I lived hundreds of miles apart. As it did for many people, playing games became a way to stay connected . The best conversations usually happen while doing something like chatting on a long drive, going on a walk, or hanging out at the beach. You couldn’t really do that in the endless Zoom parties Covid unleashed upon the world, where you’d all sit there, talking one at a time, not quite making eye contact on the screen.
Grand Theft Auto Online proved to be a rich environment for finding those kinds of activities. I think it’s the closest anything has ever gotten to feeling like an actual metaverse , where you can do just about whatever you want.
If you’ve played GTAO , you’ve probably rage-quit after getting bombed by an adolescent fighter jet pilot dressed like the prison Joker for the eighth time. That’s fair. But my brother and I usually made the mostly unconscious decision not to fight back. We’d just … hang out. Drive around. Watch the sunset. Spend hours in the in-game nightclubs, listening to real-life musicians play hour-long sets made specifically for the game. We’d go to the stores and curate outfits that felt snazzy.
Really, we are just playing dolls. GTA is a sandbox, after all, and it became the perfect space to mess around without worrying about any real stakes.
“We were brothers before, sure, but we weren’t like adult friends,” my brother told me when I asked him about GTA . “This gave us a way to spend time together and really learn more about what each other’s personality really is.”
We’ve made friends with a group in Australia who shared our approach, just hanging out in this vast virtual world and having casual conversations with the people around us. We’ve managed to convince our parents, who have never played games before, to join us. My mom—who once took our Nintendo 64 cartridge of GoldenEye 007 and smashed it with a hammer because she thought video games would make us violent—now runs around with us in GTA Online , pummeling tailgaters’ cars with a baseball bat. Despite the distance, we can spend time together in something that feels close to a real-life hang, one where we accidentally get smacked with the bat sometimes too.
It’s been a blast, and all that time spent in this virtual world starts to bleed over into the real world. I’ve sought out real-life shows of artists on the soundtrack. Sometimes an outfit would feel snazzy enough that we’d later try to replicate it in real life. One of our in-game characters got killed by a mountain lion on the same night a deer in the front yard was eviscerated by a real-life cougar.
Rockstar seems to be acutely aware of this phenomenon. (Maybe not the mountain lion bit.) What GTA does better than any other game series is spread out into the real world in surprising ways. You can see it in their marketing. Rockstar has given exclusive game clips to shows like South Park . The Weather Channel previewed the game’s advanced weather systems . Older games used music to supplement the game, but now GTA VI has become a major marketing tool for artists like Sza and Justice . Having songs in the game can garner thousands of new listeners.
“When this moment reaches enough critical mass, I think we will see this whole new model for entertainment more broadly,” says Joost van Dreunen, a video game industry analyst . “It's a little bit more of an orchestrated effort between what we play and watch and listen to and attend and connect with and share things online.”
GTA VI has excited many people for a long time. It stands to be the single greatest-selling entertainment product of all time. It’s why role-play servers are still running and populated 13 years after GTA V was released. It’s why Rockstar has invested in this creator-driven community and detailed numerous content-capture features coming to the new title. Van Dreunen says GTA VI is more like an “ operating system ” than a standard video game—a hub for people to build off of in unprecedented ways.
Like its longtime player base, the game is also bound to be much more grown up. The worlds of the GTA games have always been critical satires of certain periods. GTA VI seems keenly aware of how it is meeting the present, so much so that alt-right grifters are dedicated to calling it woke .
“ GTA used to be a very much male-dominated audience,” van Dreunen says. “It's very white in so many ways. It's a privileged lens on a lot of these social cultural issues.”
With GTA VI , all these die-hard gamers are about to start a long story where they spend half the time playing as Lucia, a Latina woman who is one of two main characters. (One of my Australian GTAO friends told me she’s very excited that Lucia is in the game, as that means better tattoos and clothing style options for female players.)
“The fans are being examined as much as GTA has historically put a lens on everything else,” van Dreunen says. “They’re pointing a mirror and critiquing the gamer audience itself.”
This feels like a particularly good time to be doing that. My brother and I, plus a billion other people, can’t wait to dive in. Lots of us will probably never be able to put it down.

The Cambridge Dictionary has named ‘human’ as the Word of the Year 2026.
The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines.
'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’.
In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay .
Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most.
"But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.”
‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”.
Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs).
Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman.
As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’. Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April.
Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common.
“AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."
Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing.
“We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion?
“All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you."
Lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary said: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.”

Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.
For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands big and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them.
Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them.
Something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case.
In a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow , an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon.
The group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care.
Vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors.
With Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover.
We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass
For products hit by recent price hikes, the new deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example.
To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. ( You can use them, too! ) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool , which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.
We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge . However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

One of NASA’s longest-tenured spacecraft is quite literally stuck in the past.
Voyager 1 , launched in September 1977 toward the outer planets of our solar system, is poised to achieve a historic milestone on Wednesday: It will be the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. The spacecraft will be so far away , that by the time its light reaches Earth, it will come from the spacecraft as it existed one day in the past. The achievement is one researchers hadn’t planned on , and yet, as Voyager 1 wades deeper into uncharted stretches of the galaxy, it continues sending back valuable scientific information.
“It's just a wonderful happenstance,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, says of the milestone. “Just as the stars were aligned for the tour of the planets, they're also aligned for this really magical, special thing that's happening for humankind.”
For Fran Bagenal, a planetary scientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder, who began working with Voyager 1 as a graduate student during its earliest years, the occasion is a momentous technological feat. “What's exciting is the fact that we have a spacecraft that was built in the mid ’70s that is still working,” she says. “Storing data on an eight-track tape that’s working on a spacecraft after 50 years—I mean, it’s amazing.”
Even as Voyager 1 approaches its 50-year anniversary next September, and its end of mission perhaps not long after that, the spacecraft is still checking items off its laundry list of scientific achievements. The spacecraft—alongside its twin, Voyager 2—was originally intended to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment to observe the outer planets .
But Voyager 1 kept traveling beyond the solar system and is now exploring the interstellar medium that fills the space between star systems. Voyager 1’s remoteness gives researchers a rare opportunity to study how the effects of the sun ripple even into the interstellar medium—and at what point those effects wane, says Jamie Rankin, deputy project scientist for the Voyager Mission at Princeton University.
Just as both Voyager spacecraft are moving through space, so is our own solar system—only about 35,000 miles per hour slower, Badaruddin says. That means that as the pair continue their journeys, they’re sending back information about the space that our own sun and planet will pass through in about three years’ time.
“We can learn from telescopes and Earth-orbiting observatories, but there's really nothing like having a spacecraft in that environment that's sending us data,” Badaruddin says.
Voyager 1’s unprecedented journey isn’t without challenges. The craft has stayed in communication with Earth far longer than planned and is trekking through regions of space that it was never built to encounter or study. Researchers are helping maintain crucial functions, but they’re now doing so with a full day of lag in communications both to and from the spacecraft, Badaruddin says.
“Light time is really affecting us,” he says. “You factor it in. It’s like having a long commute.” Building new commands for the spacecraft is now a week-long process, for instance, since it takes time to receive data from the spacecraft, analyze it, and create a new command, he adds.
Still, the Voyager team is used to navigating unforeseen circumstances. For decades, they’ve been managing to make do with a dwindling power supply coming from the craft’s nuclear generators. In September, mission operations switched off some of Voyager 1’s devices in lieu of lower-power alternatives, a maneuver the team dubbed the “Big Bang.” The swap, which saved the craft 10 watts of power, kept mission operations from having to switch off another instrument as early as next summer.
Even when contact with Voyager 1 is eventually lost, the spacecraft will leave a lasting legacy—especially for any future such far-traveling missions, should NASA or another space agency launch one. A successor to Voyager might, for instance, have new devices such as a dust instrument to better analyze the interstellar medium or cameras to give astronomers a better view of these distant stretches of the cosmos, Rankin says.
“I would hope that the Voyagers and their reaching interstellar space has taught us the lesson that we've got to just keep reaching for the stars,” she adds.
Every mission must meet its end, though. And Badaruddin’s best guess is that Voyager 1’s could come in the next three to five years, as the plutonium-238 powering it decays further. Once the craft transmits its final signal to Earth, it will still continue its silent tour of the galaxy.
But Badaruddin acknowledges he’s part of a lineage of mission managers who have said that the spacecraft only has a few years left, only to be proven wrong . “The Big Bang was a rabbit we pulled out of a hat. As long as we can keep finding rabbits, we can keep going,” he says. “Don’t bet against Voyager.”

It’s taken Voyager 1 almost 50 years to journey farther from Earth than light can travel in 24 hours.
After traveling through the void of space for 49 years, Voyager 1 has hit a momentous milestone: The spacecraft is now officially 1 light-day away from Earth, which is, as NASA put it, “very, very far.” The probe crossed the milepost on Wednesday at 5:16AM ET and is now 16.094 billion miles away from our planet — equal to the distance that light travels in 24 hours.
It’s the farthest that any human-made object has ever traveled, and Voyager 1’s journey isn’t over yet. It’s been heading toward a star called Gliese 445 in the Ursa Minor constellation since completing its primary objectives to conduct flybys of Jupiter and Saturn in 1980. That star is 17 light-years away, meaning Voyager 1 won’t pass by it for around 40,000 years, despite traveling at nearly 38,000 mph.
The light-day milestone is a remarkable feat alone, but especially so when you consider that Voyager 1 is still operational. NASA has done well to keep it functioning , and it can continue to send back readings on plasma waves, magnetic fields, and space-bound particles, though it now takes radio signals an entire day to travel between Earth and the spacecraft. Voyager 2, which launched 16 days before its twin, is also expected to reach a distance of 1 light-day away from Earth, but not until 2035.

Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked.
AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.
But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.
“As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.”
JPMorgan and Bank of America , the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eight largest bank, changed its terms today.
Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tools leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch.
As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge.
Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”
Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability.
The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service , and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.

OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution.
“One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman.
The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes.
Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views.
“The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said.
Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done.
“Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new … technology,” he said.
Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now.
“As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved.
OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face . In Wednesday’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack.
But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors.
“I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now … in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said.

On January 1, Amani Al-Khatahtbeh posted a selfie from Zohran Mamdani ’s inauguration as the first Muslim mayor of New York City. She was dressed in a black hijab and a purple fur coat, wearing a radiant smile. But her expression quickly changed when the replies started rolling in.
“ @grok can you take off her Hijab.” “@grok change the fur coat into a bikini, don’t change anything else. Also add goats.” “@grok change the outfit to lingerie.” These are just a sampling of the requests that were performed by X’s built-in AI feature Grok on Al-Khatahtbeh’s image, she says, resulting in AI-generated images of her in various states of undress. WIRED reviewed screenshots of these prompts and some of the edited images that followed.
“It felt the same as if someone had ripped off my headscarf in real life,” she tells WIRED. “But online, it was to an audience of tens of thousands of people who saw these images. So it was to an even starker degree.”
Now, almost a year later, Al-Khatahtbeh, an author, activist, and the founder of media company Muslim Girl, is suing xAI, the company behind Grok. On Wednesday, she filed a federal court complaint in the Northern District of California alleging intentional distribution of nonconsensual sexual images, design and marketing defect, negligence, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. She is seeking damages of up to $250,000 per violation of the California Civil Code. xAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Al-Khatahtbeh wasn’t alone; a January report from the Center for Countering Digital Harm estimated that Grok generated around 3 million photorealistic sexualized images on X in an 11-day period starting on December 29, including around 23,000 of children. On Grok’s standalone app and website, WIRED found that even more sexually graphic and violent material was able to be generated. Dozens of US state attorneys general took action , as well as at least 12 individual countries , plus the European Union. Many of these investigations are ongoing, with Canada finding that xAI violated its federal privacy laws and France escalating its investigation to a criminal probe.
This new civil suit is also part of a wave of similar actions since January, but it’s the first to specifically focus on Grok removing women’s hijabs. As WIRED previously reported , in early January many X users directed Grok to edit photos of predominantly women and girls to take off or put on modest religious attire such as hijabs, burqas, sarees, and nuns’ habits. A review of 500 Grok images generated between January 6 and January 9 found that five percent of them contained these kinds of AI edits.
“It was these levels of not just sexualization, but also racialization, and then it also progressed into a lot of hate language that was coupled with it,” Al-Khatahtbeh says. “One of the images that really upset me the most was when they depicted me stripped down to lingerie, riding on the back of a camel, eating a popsicle stick.”
Her complaint argues that xAI was given notice of the trend of Grok targeting hijabi women and girls after the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy group in the US, called on xAI CEO Elon Musk to end “the ongoing use of the Grok app to allegedly harass, ‘unveil,’ and create sexually explicit images of women, including prominent Muslim women.” CAIR also connected the trend to existing hostile attitudes toward “Islam, Muslims, and political causes widely supported by Muslims, such as Palestinian freedom.”
This is all too familiar to Al-Khatahtbeh, who typically goes by her first name to hundreds of thousands of social media followers. In the replies to her selfie at Mamdani’s inauguration, in addition to prompting Grok to “put her in a burqa” and other commands, dozens of replies contained violent, anti-Muslim sentiment.
Al-Khatahtbeh says the internet feels more hostile to Muslim women and girls than when she first launched her media platform more than a decade ago. “People have been equipped with more advanced ways to exercise their hate,” she says.
When the AI abuse started in January, Al-Khatahtbeh didn’t know what to do. So she called 911, and when officers arrived at her apartment, she says she showed them the photos that were being generated of her on X. They took a report, but told her they couldn’t do anything about it. Meanwhile, she reported the images on X, but she says they weren’t taken down immediately. In the days following the scrutiny over Grok’s nudification capabilities, xAI limited the ability to use these tools to paying subscribers only. But that didn’t stop the sexualized images from being created, it just meant users had to pay xAI to make them.
After confiding with women in her community, one encouraged Al-Khatahtbeh to pursue a lawsuit. Now she’s being represented by Hillary Nappi, who leads a sexual-assault practice group and has worked on amicus briefs regarding sexual exploitation on Twitter before Musk renamed it X. Nappi’s strategy in this case includes using defective product law to assert that xAI designed Grok to sexually exploit women and children. It’s a strategy that has increasingly been leveraged against big tech companies like Meta and Google to find them liable for negligent product design that harms young users.
“The only way you get some change against big tech is to sue them,” Nappi tells WIRED. “Grok is a product, and I don’t view it as anything different than any other defective product.”
In this case, Al-Khatahtbeh’s complaint asserts that xAI could and should have designed Grok to prevent users from being able to prompt the removal of religious garments like the hijab in images depicting real people. It also says Grok shouldn’t have been able to create and post “sexualized depictions of identifiable, non-consenting real people” in general.
“Because models of this kind are trained on large, uncurated image datasets, garments such as hijabs, abayas, sarees, and other modest religious dress are readily recognizable to the model, and a prompt directing their removal is trivially easy to execute unless the system is designed to refuse it,” the complaint says.
This kind of violation at the intersection of her identity as a Muslim woman is what Al-Khatahtbeh says motivated her to speak out, with the hope that she can make the internet safer for women and girls in her community.
“It does take the harm to a higher level for someone like me,” she says. “These faceless users on X shouldn’t have the ability to hop on and violate a woman on the other side of the country in this way.”

Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system.
A consultant in a local trust recently described having to work across seven bolt-on software systems for a single consultation, including one focused on billing functions. A senior US hospital administrator explained that the primary purpose of most US health data systems was to record care for reimbursement. He was astounded that, by contrast, NHS general practice records are designed to support lifelong patient care and safe prescribing, with an NHS app similarly focused on a coded healthcare rather than how much of an insurance allowance had been used up that year.
We should also ask why the NHS needs a US firm to manage its data when the UK has a strong record of healthcare-software innovation. Emis, developed with GP leadership, transformed primary care IT decades ago. Software built for an insurance market may simply not be the best fit for universal healthcare systems. Prof Caroline Mitchell GP, Sheffield, and professor of general practice research, Keele University

As Democrats flag AI bank breaches and cyber-attacks in Japan, Jay Clayton says system failures happen
A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies.
Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more.
“The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” Cantwell and Rounds wrote to Clayton, who is also serving as the White House AI czar.
“Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services,” the senators wrote.
Over the last week, tech outages at major banks, workplace communication systems and even federal infrastructure like the Federal Aviation Administration – triggering a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that grounded or delayed thousands of flights – have raised alarms about potential cyber-attacks.
Top officials have insisted the disruptions stem from software patch updates that intend to address potential AI harms.
Clayton and other national security officials told lawmakers on Wednesday that there was no indication the recent outages were the result of a malicious attack.
“Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said during the House homeland security committee hearing.
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, and Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, similarly said they had no reason to believe the outages were connected or the result of an attack.
“Many people are patching their systems. They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated,” Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday . “It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure and as you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happen.”
Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, echoed Clayton . “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” he wrote on X.
Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, attempted to quell public speculation and fear by assuring Americans that the tech outages were not linked to one another or the work of malicious actors.
But nationwide cyber outages have roiled the country, filled with voters who are already skeptical of rapidly integrating and developing AI . It is unclear what exactly has caused the widespread outages or if AI played a role.
JD Vance canceled his scheduled interview at the New York Times’ DealBook summit on Wednesday, citing his need to attend meetings addressing the recent tech outages.
Cantwell and Rounds are asking Clayton to provide cybersecurity tools to critical US infrastructure such as hospitals, utilities, small government, federal agencies and more, to prevent further disruptions.
They are also asking that US cybersecurity teams secure the same AI systems that are deployed to find vulnerabilities in software, raising concerns that they can “gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems”.

Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies , and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems. For at least one subset of hackers, it appears that era has now arrived.
Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a new wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools. These setups​​—many of which mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing techniques —use LLMs to autonomously scan potential hacking targets and attempt to force their way into poorly secured networks, then carry out attack plans written by human operators.
Dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks. The tools do not introduce new ways to attack websites or servers and are not sophisticated, according to alerts from around half a dozen security companies. Instead, they allow cybercriminals to launch attacks at speeds that would be impossible for humans to do.
Hackers also don’t need to be skilled to use the tools, researchers say, and attacks that would have taken days are completed in just hours. “Agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention,” CJ Moses, AWS’s chief information security officer, wrote in a company blog post recently.
The most prominent of these tools is Artex. Written in the programming language Go, the open-source framework was first published on GitHub in July by a pseudonymous developer using the handle Autumn-27, and it’s been spreading across some hacker communities ever since. Artex has been used across all parts of attacks, from conducting initial analysis of networks and gaining access to moving within systems and preparing data to be exported.
“It’s really an all-in-one product,” says Jacob Larsen, an offensive security researcher and founder of security firm Cypen. “Previous iterations of AI agent pen-testing tools would either only do reconnaissance—like the scanning and analysis [of targets]—and some would only do testing. This is really a point-and-shoot weapon.”
As with other AI hacking frameworks, Artex isn’t an AI product itself. Instead, it is essentially a guide that points external frontier and open-source AI models—that can be connected to it via APIs—to a series of existing penetration testing tools and processes. People using Artex or other similar setups can give simple, natural-language prompts to begin their operations. “Launch a penetration attack on [Redacted victim] to gain access to the site’s admin panel, database, or server,” one set of hackers prompted Artex, according to researchers at the security firm Check Point.
Once the instructions have been issued, multiple AI agents then carry them out. One agent will break down the plans into a series of tasks, others will try to perform these actions, and the system will then present its findings . Safety guardrails in the underlying AI models, particularly those from frontier labs, can stop hacking activity when they detect it. Increasingly, however, free Chinese and abliterated models are getting better at breaking into systems.
“It's fast; it’s efficient,” Guillaume Valadon, a researcher at security firm GitGuardian, says of Artex. Valadon and others say the simplicity of the tools makes it easier for unskilled wannabe hackers to try to enter the market—even if they have no clue about what they’re doing. “It lowers the bar,” Valadon says. “I would say my grandmother can do it, except that she doesn't have a laptop, but the bar is that low.”
As a result, a flurry of reports from cybersecurity companies have linked Artex use to attempted and successful hacks—often by Chinese-speaking cybercriminals trying to make money. These include the theft of personal information from thousands of South Korean financial institutions, potential cryptocurrency theft, and hunting for exposed login details on GitHub.
“A variety of malicious cyber actors have used Artex to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, health care, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI warned in an alert about Artex last week.
In October, China-linked hackers known as Vapor Panda used Artex to target more than 200 organizations, including think tanks, semiconductor and defense firms in the US, and government foreign ministries in Europe and elsewhere, according to security firm CrowdStrike. Microsoft spotted Chinese hackers that it tracks as Storm-0940 using Artex to try to sign in to Microsoft 365 setups following a supply chain attack . It took hackers less than three hours to gain privileged access to systems.
On October 8, the Autumn-27 developer removed Artex from GitHub, stating in a comment that they are “no way associated with these malicious attacks” and that the tools were developed for “educational and research purposes.” An email WIRED sent to an address linked to the developer did not receive a response.
Despite the developer pulling Artex, multiple versions of the framework have been copied and continue to be developed and used, alongside other similar tools. Valadon says GitGuardian has documented 45 different AI attack frameworks so far, with CyberstrikeAI, Hexstrike, CAIRN, and PentAGI being frequently mentioned by researchers. They all work in similar ways, with some slightly different technical capabilities. One silver lining for people defending against attacks using such tools is that they’re currently easy to spot.
“These tools are not stealthy right now,” says Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at internet security firm Censys. Many of the attacks create a lot of noise in systems—making thousands of probes in quick succession. For instance, agentic coding platform Dosu said Artex was used to send 80,000 requests to its systems in just 90 minutes. Researchers say that basic security fundamentals—patching software, not using default credentials or exposing secrets , and monitoring for unusual network activity—can help defend against many of the approaches from those using Artex.
Pinpointing the number of cybercriminals using Artex and other frameworks isn’t easy; however, thousands of instances of the systems being set up have been exposed to the internet, according to analysis by Censys and the Shadowserver Foundation. Perhaps hinting at the sophistication of those using Artex, researchers have found multiple instances of the tool left unsecured and fully open to the internet, allowing them to inspect how operators are using it.
Last week, Cutler says, two exposed Artex servers appeared to show Chinese native speakers targeting other Chinese entities. “In one of the cases, it was a university that was being targeted with a password spraying attack, and it has all of that vibe of a student trying to change their grades,” he says.
“There is a level of this activity that’s occurring that is likely organized, sophisticated, criminal activity,” Cutler says. “There is also, in parallel, likely a subset of the activity that falls more into that juvenile crime realm.”

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are holding talks in Shenzhen, a day before a one-of-its-kind trilateral summit with US President Donald Trump in the southern Chinese city.
Chinese and Russian news agencies reported that the two leaders began talks around midday on Wednesday.
It was their fifth meeting this year, one of which took place by video link.
Thursday’s meeting has raised concern in Kyiv and European capitals that the three leaders could settle Ukraine’s future without them and divide the world into modern spheres of influence.
Washington initially said Ukraine was not expected to be on the agenda, but Trump later said it would be. Xi regards the war as not China’s concern.
Beijing has said only that the leaders will hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations” on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting.
According to Washington, the Iran war and nuclear disarmament are also on the table after the US-Russia bilateral nuclear weapons treaty expired in February. China has long argued that the US and Russia should cut their much larger arsenals before it will discuss limits on its own.
Opening the event, Xi called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence and free trade. China would pursue “deep-seated reform”, he said, starting with lower tariffs, wider market access and work on regulation and management standards.
Putin, who has been shunned by the West since he invaded Ukraine in 2022, told the APEC gathering he expected the trilateral to be “highly useful”.
With military and political risks rising, he said, “what is desperately needed is unity rather than division... and dialogue rather than ultimatums.”
He also argued that Western sanctions had failed, saying they could not fully halt growth or wreck the economies of rival states.
Trump was still in the Philippines on Wednesday, where he attended a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). A day earlier he met fellow Quad leaders from Australia, Japan and India for the first time in his second term. The group is broadly seen as a counterweight to Chinese influence in the region.
He said he hoped to hold one-on-one talks with both Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Shenzhen, adding that Kim “would like” to meet in China.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Manila, stopped short of confirming a Kim meeting but said engagement was the only way to resolve problems with North Korea.
Around 2,000 people protested during Trump’s visit, carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica”, a reference to a US supply chain initiative.

Huang, Nvidia yönetim kurulunun uygun görmesi halinde CEO olarak şirkete dönmekten “onur duyacağını” söyledi. Huang, X üzerinden yaptığı açıklamada Nvidia'nın hayatının işi olduğunu belirterek, görevinden ayrılmasının ardından çalışanlardan, yatırımcılardan, iş ortaklarından ve müşterilerden geri dönmesi yönünde çok sayıda mesaj aldığını ifade etti. Jones, Huang'ın şirketin davranış kuralları, standartları ve kurum kültürüyle uyumlu olmayan kişisel davranışlarının ortaya çıkmasının ardından başkanlık, CEO'luk ve yönetim kurulu üyeliği görevlerinden gönüllü olarak ayrıldığını belirtti.
Nvidia'da CEO'luk görevini geçici olarak şirketin CFO'su ve başkan yardımcısı Colette Kress yürütüyor. Yönetim kurulu ise kalıcı CEO için hem şirket içinden hem de dışarıdan adayları değerlendiriyor.
Nvidia yönetim kurulu aynı zamanda şirketin ulusal güvenlik ve ihracat kontrollerine ilişkin süreçlerini denetlemek için yeni bir komite oluşturdu . Komitenin başkanlığını Nvidia yönetim kurulu üyesi ve Goldman Sachs'ın eski başkan yardımcısı Suzanne Nora Johnson üstlenecek.
Reuters'a göre bu hamle, Huang'ın ayrılmasının ardından Nvidia'nın yönetim yapısında attığı ilk önemli adımlardan biri oldu. ABD'li yetkililer özellikle Huang'ın eski Megaspeed yöneticisi Alice Huang ile ilişkisini ve Megaspeed'in kısıtlamalara tabi Nvidia çiplerinin Çin'e yönlendirilmesinde rol oynayıp oynamadığını inceliyor. Wall Street Journal'ın aktardığı bilgilere göre ABD Menkul Kıymetler ve Borsa Komisyonu (SEC) da Nvidia hakkında bir inceleme yürütüyor. Öte yandan Huang'ın yeniden göreve getirilmesi için çalışanlar, yatırımcılar ve teknoloji dünyasından isimlerin destek verdiği bir kampanya da yürütülüyor. Buna rağmen Nvidia yönetim kurulunun son açıklaması, şirketin şimdilik Huang sonrası döneme ve yeni bir kalıcı CEO arayışına odaklandığını gösteriyor.

“ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.”
United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply.
“ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement . “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.”
The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket’s failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle’s main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin.
This represents an important revelation from ULA and will provide some major relief to different parts of the US aerospace community, particularly Blue Origin and NASA.
That’s because the BE-4 engine is also the bedrock of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket. This powerful rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that was later attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
After this anomaly, Blue Origin retrofitted the main oxygen valve, including for Vulcan missions. Now it’s clear that this retrofit was not implicated in the Vulcan accident. With the preliminary Vulcan investigation having largely exonerated the BE-4 engine, Blue Origin can press ahead with its return-to-flight mission with New Glenn, which could occur as soon as January.
“Following the Vulcan anomaly, Blue Origin immediately worked alongside ULA to review flight data and support the investigation,” Blue Origin said in a statement Wednesday. “Together, we identified that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines. ULA is a valued partner, and we look forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.”
Amid a worsening US launch crunch, New Glenn offers the most tangible option for near-term relief for satellite operators, including Amazon Leo, which lost dozens of satellites on Sunday. The heavy-lift rocket has many commercial and government customers lined up for launch. NASA in particular is counting on the rocket to launch a number of lunar missions in the next two years, as well as play a significant role in landing humans on the Moon later this decade.
Also a relief to NASA will be confirmation that Vulcan’s upper stage, the Centaur V, did not contribute to the failure. NASA recently contracted with ULA to use the Centaur V as its new upper stage for the Space Launch System rocket, enabling future missions to the Moon.
For ULA, however, the latest update only brings more challenges.
Vulcan represents the company’s great hope to remain relevant in a US launch industry increasingly dominated by SpaceX and newer entrants such as Blue Origin. With Vulcan on the sidelines, other companies, such as Relativity Space, Rocket Lab, and Stoke Space, could also elbow out the once all-powerful launch firm.
Although Sunday’s Vulcan flight, its fifth overall, was the first outright mission failure for the rocket, two previous launches also experienced problems. Those issues involved the nozzle of the solid rocket boosters. ULA has now spent three years trying to move the rocket out of its teething phase and into regular operations. A successful launch on Sunday could have set up at least a monthly launch cadence next year.
Now, the cash-strapped company must also contend with a new issue involving propellant management and complicated plumbing that feeds liquid oxygen and methane to the BE-4 engines. It will certainly be offline for several months.
